results.body_snippet:
## Summary

There are now many open Codex reports describing a common **user-visible symptom family**:

> Codex subscription quota or purchased credits are depleted materially faster than the user's prior baseline or local/token evidence would predict, sometimes with abrupt changes during an unchanged usage window, passive/background consumption, or usage records that do not reconcile with the meter.

This meta issue is intended to **link and compare those reports in one place**.

**This does not assume they all have one root cause.** The evidence already points to several potentially independent mechanisms: entitlement/provisioning, server-side weighting/accounting, background activity, retries/polling, context replay, analytics/ledger gaps, and client-side workflow amplification. The purpose is to stop treating each report as an isolated anecdote and give maintainers a single place to correlate timelines, fixes, regressions, and account-side reconciliation.

# Elsa Roadmap

Last refreshed: 2026-09-16 (post-3.8.2 operational patches and BPMN authoring status)

This roadmap is a product direction document, not a fixed release calendar. Elsa is developed through a mix of core maintainer work, customer-funded work, and community contributions, so sequencing can change when real-world demand changes. The intent is stable: make Elsa the most productive, dependable, and extensible workflow platform for the .NET ecosystem.

This version is grounded in the current `elsa-core`, `elsa-studio`, and `elsa-extensions` repositories, including source code, open issues, open pull requests, releases, and discussions where available.

Elsa should feel like the natural workflow engine for .NET teams:

- productive enough for application developers to model real business processes quickly
- dependable enough for production operations, rolling deploys, multi-tenant systems, and distributed workloads
- open enough to embed, customize, extend, and automate without fighting the framework
- powerful enough to connect systems, run long-lived processes, expose human tasks, and observe what is happening

results.title: [Feature] Per-pane auto git worktree + branch isolation (dmux-style agent isolation)
results.body_snippet:
## Summary

Add a first-class, built-in option where **opening a new pane (or workspace) automatically creates a dedicated git worktree on a fresh branch**, so each agent (Claude / Codex / etc.) runs in a fully isolated checkout. Closing the pane reclaims the worktree (with a safe snapshot path for recovery).

This is the UX [dmux](https://github.com/standardagents/dmux) ships out of the box: *"every pane gets its own git worktree and branch, and agents work in complete isolation."*

## Motivation

Running N agents in parallel against the same checkout is the core value-prop of cmux's claude-teams / multi-agent flow, but today the user has to wire worktrees themselves. Concretely:

- The currently documented path is the [`worktree-agents` custom command](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux/blob/main/web/app/%5Blocale%5D/docs/custom-commands/page.tsx) — a shell snippet the user pastes into `cmux.json`. It works but:
  - Not discoverable (you have to know the docs page exists).
  - No lifecycle: nothing cleans the worktree on close, nothing snapshots on crash, nothing tracks which pane owns which worktree.

results.title: Proposal: Sunset repo-updater
results.body_snippet:
# Proposal

Today, repo-updater is serving too many concerns, while being a singleton instance, without failure and resource isolation between those different concerns.

Any nil pointer panic, or memory leak, or any other noisy neighbor issue will cause a cascading failure of unrelated features owned by different teams.

We got to this situation because there was an unmet need of a place to run background jobs, and repo-updater made that easy, so more and more use cases have been integrated into this singleton service over time. The more things we add to repo-updater, the higher the chance of cascading failure.

In contrast, the Code Intelligence team has created completely separate services for the background jobs they have. While it would be a possibility to separate all of these different concerns into separate services, we must consider the overhead which that would force upon us — more things to monitor, build, deploy and provision.

To avoid that overhead and address the issues at hand, I propose that we introduce a new service called `worker`, and extract the different concerns that currently live in repo-updater. Some of those would end up in `worker`, others else

Nebari's current governance was written for **Nebari Classic** - a single, monolithic data science platform shipped from one repository. The project has moved to the **Nebari Kubernetes Platform (NKP)**: a stable infrastructure core (Nebari Infrastructure Core, "NIC") plus a growing set of independently-developed **Software Packs**, each in its own repository.

results.title: DataStore transaction support
results.body_snippet:
DataStore might benefit from transaction support, for both internal and external use cases. E.g.:

* A customer may want to save multiple related records, rolling back locally if not successful, and in sync-enabled installations, only publishing to API if all are successful
* Populating the outgoing mutation queue is currently separate from the data store `save` operation that writes the original record. It would be a more robust customer experience to wrap the mutation queue and save operation in a transaction so the whole thing could be atomically failed if one part fails
* As noted in this code snippet, reconciling incoming mutations has much the same use case: it must apply changes to the local datastore and also update the mutation queue record. Those are related and would benefit from transaction semantics
https://github.com/aws-amplify/amplify-ios/blob/4cb4423a6eb3d46dc0caf4bf55392384b0e4acc8/AmplifyPlugins/DataStore/AWSDataStoreCategoryPlugin/Sync/SubscriptionSync/ReconcileAndLocalSave/ReconcileAndLocalSaveOperation.swift#L201-L206

results.title: Graph-Driven Validation for Gateway API Reconciler
results.body_snippet:
# Graph-Driven Validation for Gateway API Reconciler

## Problem

The Gateway API reconciler validates route and listener attachment across four phases that reimplement the same checks. Each core check, such as parentRef matching, namespace filtering, or hostname intersection, is re-implemented up to seven different times. The copies drift apart and cause bugs. For example, after merging TCP/UDP Route, [this follow up bug fix was needed immediately](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/46363) to perform the re-validation necessary within the translation layer.

Namespace filtering is a good example of this pattern. A listener's `AllowedRoutes.Namespaces` selector is evaluated in at least five places (`isAllowed`, `listenerisAllowed`, `CheckGatewayAllowedForNamespace`, `routeAllowedByParent`, and  `IsListenerNamespaceAllowed`), and they have divergent logic. A `namespacesPreFiltered` flag skips the check for ListenerSet listeners whose namespaces are already resolved, but Gateway-listeners cannot use this path because they have not been filtered in the reconciler context.

The validation phases also disagree on which check is authoritative. The filter `filterHTTPRoutesByListener` c

results.title: Unreal Azeroth is not for EVERYONE
results.body_snippet: # Unreal Azeroth Is Not for Everyone The website says it plainly: *"Legacy Mode goes live for everyone. This is the full vanilla world, playable from day one."* For everyone. A World of Warcraft client *"written from scratch in Unreal Engine 5"*, with built-in anti-cheat, presented as a non-commercial, community-driven, volunteer project. When you take it apart, you find something else. These protections are not aimed at cheaters. They are anti-reverse-engineering and anti-private-server protections whose actual purpose is simple: prevent a player from connecting to a server that does not have an Unreal Azeroth license. No license, no connection, for anyone. What follows are the discrepancies between what is presented publicly and what the code actually does, one by one. ## "For Everyone", Except Without a License *"Legacy Mode goes live for everyone."* On paper, it is open. In practice, it is not. The client cannot connect to anything without a series of server-side keys. No keys, no connection. And these keys are not held by the players; they are held by authorized servers.
